1: # ODB - ORM for C++
2: 
3: ODB is an open-source, cross-platform, and cross-database object-relational
4: mapping (ORM) system for C++. It allows you to persist C++ classes to a
5: relational database without having to deal with tables, columns, or SQL and
6: without manually writing any mapping code. ODB supports the MySQL, SQLite,
7: PostgreSQL, Oracle, and Microsoft SQL Server relational databases. It also
8: comes with optional profiles for Boost and Qt which allow you to seamlessly
9: use value types, containers, and smart pointers from these libraries in your
10: persistent C++ classes.
11: 
12: For further information, including licensing conditions, documentation, and
13: binary packages, refer to the [ODB project
14: page](https://codesynthesis.com/products/odb/).
15: 
16: NOTE: the steps described below are more appropriate for the development of
17: ODB as opposed to consumption. In case you just want to use ODB:
18: 
19: * If you want to use a binary package, see the [ODB download
20:   page](https://codesynthesis.com/products/odb/download.xhtml).
21: 
22: * If you want to build ODB from source and use the result from a project that
23:   uses a build system other than `build2`, then see [Installing ODB with
24:   `build2`](https://codesynthesis.com/products/odb/doc/install-build2.xhtml)
25:   for the step-by-step instructions.
26: 
27: * If you want to use ODB from a project that uses `build2` as the build
28:   system, then see the accompanying `PACKAGE-README.md` file.
29: 
30: The development setup for ODB uses multiple build configurations: a single
31: host configuration for the ODB compiler and a target configuration per
32: database (or multiple databases). For example:
33: 
34: ```
35: git clone .../odb.git
36: cd odb
37: 
38: bdep init --empty
39: 
40: bdep config create @host   ../odb-host --type host cc config.cxx=g++
41: bdep config create @sqlite ../odb-sqlite cc config.cxx=g++
42: bdep config create @pgsql  ../odb-pgsql  cc config.cxx=g++
43: bdep config create @mysql  ../odb-mysql  cc config.cxx=g++
44: bdep config create @oracle ../odb-oracle cc config.cxx=g++
45: bdep config create @mssql  ../odb-mssql  cc config.cxx=g++
46: 
47: bdep init @host -d odb
48: bdep init @sqlite -d libodb -d libodb-sqlite -d odb-tests -d odb-examples
49: bdep init @pgsql  -d libodb -d libodb-pgsql  -d odb-tests -d odb-examples
50: bdep init @mysql  -d libodb -d libodb-mysql  -d odb-tests -d odb-examples
51: bdep init @oracle -d libodb -d libodb-oracle -d odb-tests -d odb-examples
52: bdep init @mssql  -d libodb -d libodb-mssql  -d odb-tests -d odb-examples
53: ```
54: 
55: Note that while the target configurations can use any compiler (and you can
56: create multiple such configurations for different compilers), the host
57: configuration must use GCC with plugin support enabled because the ODB
58: compiler is implemented as a GCC plugin. GCC plugin headers are usually
59: distributed as a separate package which is not installed by default. To
60: install it on Debian and alike distributions (where `N` is the GCC major
61: version):
62: 
63: ```
64: apt-get install gcc-N-plugin-dev
65: ```
66: 
67: To install it on Fedora and alike distributions:
68: 
69: ```
70: dnf install gcc-plugin-devel
71: ```

18: compiler), `libodb` (the common runtime library), and `libodb-<database>` (the

43: depends: libodb-boost ^2.5.0
